answer_md:
🐾 Here’s the story behind Matt’s payments work at **JP Morgan Chase**.

From **August 2009 to June 2012**, Matt served as Technology Delivery Lead for ACCESS Next Generation, the bank’s unified corporate banking portal. The challenge went beyond replacing an interface: regional payment systems had different formats, client configurations, entitlement structures, and regulatory requirements. Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform provided the foundation, but the bank needed payment capabilities well beyond its out-of-box offering.

Matt managed a blended team of **40+** **Accenture** and **JP Morgan Chase** resources across the US, Mumbai, and Bangalore. He spent **70 to 80%** of his time embedded at Bottomline’s Portsmouth offices, managing the boundary between platform configuration and bespoke engineering.

He designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and tax payment modules. That included NACHA file validation, foreign-exchange rate visibility, and Message Authentication Code security so corporate users could verify payment integrity before release. He also built payment-type-specific permissions, such as allowing wire approval without permitting FX initiation, and contextual help explaining payment fields and compliance requirements.

Alongside the payment engine, Matt designed the centralized gateway for message transformation, protocol translation, and routing across **12 countries**, replacing fragmented point-to-point integrations. He redesigned user administration with role-based profiles and bulk permission changes, reducing entitlement management from days to minutes.

Matt also led payments data migration without disruption to live payment operations. For the global rollout, he translated jurisdiction-specific requirements into data visibility and access controls, sequencing regional launches by regulatory readiness rather than using a single big-bang deployment. He owned on-call and severity-one incident response across releases and migrations.

ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, consolidating regional systems into a single portal serving **135,000+** corporations, financial institutions, governments, and municipalities across **180+ countries**. The regional compliance framework enabled rollout across APAC, EMEA, and the Americas without regulatory blockers.

🐾 Here’s how Matt describes his leadership philosophy.

Matt leads with empathy, clarity, and purpose. He builds a “permit to fail” learning environment and balanced teams: Product + Engineering + Design together. His aim is to create an environment where engineers, designers, and product teams can do the best work of their careers.

Most engineering teams he inherited were stuck: over-processed, under-trusted, and waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes. At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Center, fear of blame kept teams from experimenting, while hierarchical structures and role silos created bottlenecks and slower delivery.

Matt made intent explicit and pushed decisions to the people closest to the work. He used transparency, direct feedback, and open communication, and coached teams to think clearly rather than just execute tasks. Instead of pointing fingers when something failed, he organized non-punitive post-mortems and carried lessons into subsequent sprints. Teams tested assumptions through lean, low-stakes experiments before committing to costly builds.

He assembled balanced teams of engineers, product managers, and UX architects with equal participation and shared accountability. Pair programming, collaborative coding, retrospectives, automation, and continuous delivery were part of daily work. Teams could voice feedback and implement changes autonomously.

At the Cloud Innovation Center, teams achieved **4x delivery acceleration** once they embraced lean product and modern engineering practices. In the balanced-team work, teams reduced handoffs and project delays and achieved **zero-defect production code** through iterative development and real-time feedback loops.

Matt’s work spans Execution & Delivery, Org & Working-Model Transformation, and Talent & Enablement: shipping enterprise platforms, changing how teams build software, and building the organization that delivers them.

New hires also needed hands-on experience with cloud-native technologies and modern engineering practices.

Across the CIC practice, results included **4X faster velocity**, **zero-defect deployments**, and **10-person teams** delivering equivalent output to traditional **20-person teams**. At **JP Morgan**, teams outpaced peer velocity within the first **2 sprints**. The centers delivered **30+ product engagements** across **15+ Fortune 500 clients** and contributed to **\$100M+ in repeat business** through delivery excellence and customer relationships.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s a time Matt failed, and what happened afterward.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a financial services client. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with existing documentation.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup. Instead of verifying the configuration, he assumed the IAM controls and environment boundaries were correct. He relied on inherited documentation without confirming its accuracy, did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, and did not verify whether production customer data had been masked or scrubbed. He also had not implemented compensating controls such as email interception.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. The team identified insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed from downstream environments.

The client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described it as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.”

Afterward, Matt made IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach. His own wording for the lesson was: “assumptions are risks in disguise.”

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt built AWS Launchpad.

At **Accenture’s** Liquid Studio, traditional training programs couldn’t keep pace with rapidly evolving AWS technologies. Engineers had gaps in cloud competency, and cloud adoption was slowing. The Atlanta Innovation Hub needed a structured program that would prepare engineers for cloud-native transformation initiatives, not just certification exams.

As Cloud Native Architecture Lead, Matt led AWS Launchpad from **July 2018 to November 2019**, developing the program in collaboration with AWS. He designed structured learning paths and certification programs around AWS core services and cloud-native application development. The curriculum included Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB, Kubernetes, and ECS/Fargate.

Rather than relying on theory alone, Matt delivered interactive workshops and hands-on labs that immersed engineers in real-world AWS environments. Engineers could apply what they were learning as they worked through the program. He also established cloud expert mentorship teams to embed AWS best practices and retain institutional knowledge, giving participants support beyond the training sessions.

Matt organized group coaching sessions and knowledge-sharing workshops alongside those learning paths. The program combined structured study, practical application, and mentor-based training to build cloud competencies across **Accenture**, with certification as part of that broader enablement effort.

More than **200 professionals earned AWS certifications**, including AWS Solutions Architect and DevOps Engineer certifications. The program accelerated cloud adoption and the launch of cloud-native initiatives, while establishing mentorship and knowledge-sharing practices for continued learning across teams.
